original_value: Pesticides are heavily used in agriculture to protect crops from diseases, insects, and weeds. However, only a fraction of the used pesticides reaches the target and the rest slips through the soil, causing the contamination of ground- and surface water resources. Given the emerging interest in the on-site detection of analytes that can replace traditional chromatographic techniques, alternative methods for pesticide measuring have recently encountered remarkable attention. This review gives a focused overview of the literature related to the electrochemical detection of selected pesticides. Here, we focus on the electrochemical detection of three important pesticides; glyphosate, lindane and bentazone using a variety of electrochemical detection techniques, electrode materials, electrolyte media, and sample matrix. The review summarizes the different electrochemical studies and provides an overview of the analytical performances reported such as; the limits of detection and linearity range. This article highlights the advancements in pesticide detection of the selected pesticides using electrochemical methods and point towards the challenges and needed efforts to achieve electrochemical detection suitable for on-site applications.

result.paraphrase: Pesticides are widely applied in agriculture to safeguard crops against diseases, insects, and weeds. Yet only a portion of the applied pesticide reaches its intended target, while the remainder percolates through soil and contaminates ground and surface water resources. With growing interest in on-site analyte detection as an alternative to conventional chromatographic methods, new approaches for pesticide measurement have recently drawn considerable attention. This review presents a concentrated overview of the literature on electrochemical detection of selected pesticides. It focuses on three key pesticides—glyphosate, lindane, and bentazone—using diverse electrochemical detection techniques, electrode materials, electrolyte media, and sample matrices. The review also summarizes the reported analytical performances, including limits of detection and linearity ranges. Overall, the article highlights progress in electrochemical pesticide detection and identifies the challenges and necessary efforts needed to make these methods suitable for on-site applications.
